intro: Simple Host puts websites online. Your own AI app or agent makes the site; Simple Host gives it an address, saved data, visitor sign-in, and the controls you need to run it.

This page is the map: every area of the product, the features inside each one, and where to read more. Simple Hack, which runs hackathons on simple-hack.app, is the same software run as its own product and has its own branch below.

root.name: Simple Host
root.line: Hosting for the sites your AI made

areas.title: Sites and deploy
areas.line: Your AI app sends the finished site to Simple Host, which puts it online and keeps it there, with versions, a copy to download, and an undo for delete.

features.name: Publish a page directly
features.line: Send the page itself, the HTML and anything alongside it, and it is live in seconds with no build step or upload dialog.
features.who: Anyone with a finished page, and every AI agent publishing on your behalf.
features.how: Your AI app sends the files in one request. Text files go in `files`; images, fonts, and other binaries go base64-encoded in `files_base64` in the same request. The site is live at its address as soon as the request returns. A site must include a home page.
features.example: A consultant asks their chat app for a one-page rate card with a contact form; the app writes the page and publishes it in the same turn.
features.where: Whatever your AI does when you say "publish this".
features.limits: Script files are refused. Each upload is capped by the per-upload size limit (see Publish a whole folder; Simple Hack allows 25 MB). A site must include a home page.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack team sites use the same route with a 25 MB upload limit.
features.evidence: features.html #deploy-inline-files; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (POST/PUT /v1/sites/{sitename}/files, inline JSON, base64 allowed); FEATURES.md L90 (Hack 25 MB). Not rendered.

features.name: Publish a whole folder
features.line: Hand over a zipped folder, the output of a normal web build with images and fonts, and the whole thing goes live at once.
features.who: Anyone with a real project rather than a single page: a built site, a portfolio, a documentation folder.
features.how: A coding agent packages the folder as a tar.gz or zip and sends it in one upload. The upload becomes a new version and is live when it finishes. Shrink photos to about 1600 px wide, using WebP or JPEG at about 80% quality; phone photos are often 4 to 12 MB. Keep zip files, installers, and videos elsewhere and link to them.
features.example: An agency builds a client's marketing site with a static site generator and has its agent publish the `dist` folder after each round of changes.
features.where: No screen for it. Point your agent at the folder and it packages and sends it.
features.limits: Up to **100 MB** per upload. Operator exceptions apply. New websites from 5 October 2026 may use 200 MB including kept versions, and an account 1 GB; older sites have no total cap, and saved data and storage resources are counted separately. Script files are refused outright; anything that looks like a stored secret or a hidden settings file is silently left out without telling you. Remove files you no longer use and delete old sites you do not need.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack allows 25 MB per upload; a small box has no total cap unless its operator sets one.
features.evidence: features.html #deploy-archive (all facts kept; the en-dash range of phone photo sizes rewritten as '4 to 12 MB'); FEATURES.md §1 L84-90 and Limits row; FEATURES.md §18 L2328 (MAX_ARCHIVE_MB default 100); PARITY row 'Upload validation'. Not rendered.

features.name: Republish over the same site
features.line: Publishing again to the same name replaces what visitors see at once, at the same address.
features.who: Anyone iterating, which is everyone, after the first day.
features.how: Your AI app sends the new files to the same site name. The new version goes live immediately and the earlier version is kept, so you can go back to it. A republish replaces the whole site; to change a few files and leave the rest, see Change a few files.
features.example: A restaurant updates its menu prices every month by telling its chat app what changed; the app republishes and the address stays the same.
features.where: Your AI does it when you ask for a change.
features.limits: A republish replaces the whole site, it does not merge. Anything you leave out disappears from the live version, though the old version is still kept.
features.evidence: features.html #deploy-update; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (PUT /v1/sites/{sitename}); PARITY row 'Sites: deploy, versions, rollback, delete'. Not rendered.

features.name: Change a few files of a site
features.line: Send only the files that changed and keep everything else live as it is, so a one-line fix does not resend the whole site.
features.who: Anyone making small edits to a site that already has many pages or photos.
features.how: Your AI app reads only the files it is about to change, then sends them with the instruction to keep the other live files. It can also name files to remove. The result is a new version with the rest of the site unchanged. The merge happens under the site's lock, so two edits never half-apply.
features.example: A clinic changes its opening hours on one page of a twelve-page site; the agent sends that one file and the photos and other pages stay exactly as they were.
features.where: Ask your AI app. It uses `update_site` with `keep_other_files` and `remove_files`.
features.limits: The same size and entry limits as a full publish apply to the merged result, and the site must still have a home page afterwards.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §1 MCP tools row (update_site keep_other_files, remove_files); FEATURES.md L935 (PUT .../files?keep=1); FEATURES.md L933 (patch sanitized, site lock held through merge); PARITY row 'Change a few files of a site' (same; must keep an index.html). Hack and small box: not stated, same binary. Not rendered.

features.name: Publish from CI in one call
features.line: One call creates the site the first time and publishes a new version after that, so a build pipeline can publish on every push.
features.who: Anyone whose site lives in a repository with a build step.
features.how: Create a Deploy only key and save it as the pipeline's secret. The pipeline sends the built folder with the create flag set; if the site does not exist yet it is created, otherwise a new version goes live. A plain create of a name that already exists is refused with a message naming the right call. GitHub Actions and the like work this way on every push.
features.example: A product team keeps its documentation in a repository; every merge to main rebuilds the docs and publishes them to the same address.
features.where: No screen. Create a Deploy only key in the Keys panel, save it as the pipeline's secret, and your agent writes the workflow.
features.limits: A deploy key can create, update, roll back, and list sites, and nothing else. It cannot set the versions kept or the passcode. A deploy key can publish code that runs when you open your own site; treat it like the site itself.
features.editions_note: Enterprise spells the create flag `?create=true` where simple-host.app uses `?create=1`.
features.evidence: features.html #deploy-ci; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (?create=1, 409 site_exists, 404 says add ?create=1; keep-versions and lock not for deploy-only keys); PARITY row 'Deploy from CI in one call'. Hack and small box: not stated, same routes. Not rendered.

features.name: Upload link for a big archive
features.line: When a site is too large to send inline, your agent gets a one-time link and uploads the tar.gz or zip to it from a shell.
features.who: Coding agents with a shell publishing a built site with many images or fonts.
features.how: The agent asks for an upload link for the site, then uploads the archive to it. The link creates the site or publishes a new version, works once, for one site, for 15 minutes, and checks your sign-in again at upload time. The upload meets the usual size, scope, and storage checks.
features.example: A developer's coding agent builds a photographer's portfolio with 60 MB of images and uploads the archive through the link instead of pasting files into the chat.
features.where: Ask your AI app. It calls `create_upload_link` with `archive: true`.
features.limits: 15 minutes, one use, one site. At most 20 live links per account. Links stop working when you sign out, disconnect the app, or your sign-in expires. Never share the link or put it in a page.
features.editions_note: On Simple Hack the upload link is the default form of `create_upload_link`; Enterprise does not have upload links.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md L939 (archive: true, PUT /v1/uploads/{token}, 15 minutes, 20 links, upload_link_signed_out); PARITY row 'Connector archive upload links' (Hack by default; Enterprise not built). Small box: not stated, same binary. Not rendered.

features.name: You choose the site name
features.line: The name you pick becomes the last part of the address, so it is worth choosing something readable.
features.who: Anyone publishing anything.
features.how: Your AI app asks for a name or picks one when it publishes. The name must be free on your account and is checked against a reserved list. You can rename the site later without republishing it.
features.example: A bakery asks for `menu` rather than `site-2`, so its address reads as the menu it is.
features.where: Your AI asks or picks one when it publishes; ask it for a different one any time.
features.limits: Lower-case letters, numbers, and dashes only. Reserved names are refused. You can rename it later (Rename under Manage on your sites page); see Rename a site for what happens to the old name.
features.evidence: features.html #site-name; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (?create=1: reserved name check). The old page's redirect clause is kept in #site-rename, since addresses and legacy redirects belong to another area. Not rendered.

features.name: Pages only: nothing runs on the server
features.line: What you publish is served back exactly as it is; your scripts run in the visitor's browser and nothing you upload executes on the server.
features.who: Everyone: it is why an AI-written site is safe to host here without review.
features.how: Simple Host serves your files as static pages. Your page's own JavaScript runs in the visitor's browser as normal. Forms, bookings, and saved entries work through the site's saved data and storage, which the pages call from the browser.
features.example: A startup's pitch page with a waitlist form runs entirely in the browser and saves entries to the site's storage; there is no server code to maintain.
features.where: Not a setting. It is how publishing works.
features.limits: No server-side languages, no databases you install, no background jobs. If your idea needs a server that runs your code, this is not the right home for it.
features.evidence: features.html #static-only (one banned adverb dropped from the Where text per voice rules); FEATURES.md §1 lead (static site upload). Not rendered.

features.name: Up to a hundred sites
features.line: One account can hold up to a hundred separate sites, so experiments do not need a second account.
features.who: Anyone who builds a lot of small things.
features.how: Every site you create counts toward the cap, including sites in Recently deleted until they are purged, so a restore never needs a check. The connector reports your cap, and your AI app can tell you how many sites you have.
features.example: A freelancer keeps a separate site per client proposal and still has room for their own portfolio and tools.
features.where: No screen shows your count against the limit; you find out when publishing is refused, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: **100 sites** on simple-host.app. Sites in Recently deleted count until they are purged. Delete something to make room.
features.editions_note: The 100-site figure is simple-host.app's; Enterprise and self-hosted instances set their own site quota, and Enterprise also caps stored bytes per owner.
features.evidence: features.html #site-quota; FEATURES.md §1 Limits row (100 sites, MAX_SITES_PER_ACCOUNT, Recently deleted counts, /v1/me reports max_sites); PARITY row 'Quotas' (Enterprise QUOTA_MAX_SITES + QUOTA_MAX_BYTES). Hack: not stated, team sites follow the event. Not rendered.

features.name: Website file allowances
features.line: A new site may use 200 MB including its kept versions, an account 1 GB, and a refused publish leaves the live site untouched.
features.who: Anyone publishing photo-heavy pages, and anyone whose publish was refused for size.
features.how: Three limits apply to website files. Each upload may be at most 100 MB. A website created on or after 5 October 2026 may use 200 MB in total for its live files and all kept versions. An account may use 1 GB for all its website files and kept versions, including sites in Recently deleted until they are purged. The check runs before anything is written, using the size after old versions are pruned, so a refused publish changes nothing. Your sites page and your AI app show the same usage figures and the same tips.
features.example: A real-estate agent publishing listing photos keeps them at about 1600 px wide and 80% quality, so twenty listings fit comfortably under the site's 200 MB.
features.where: Usage and tips appear on your sites page and in your AI app's replies; a refused publish says which limit it hit, the current size, and what to do.
features.limits: Sites created before 5 October 2026 have no total cap. Saved data and KV, SQLite, and file storage have their own limits and do not count toward either file cap. For personal photos use Add photos, which makes small copies on your device. Keep zip files, installers, and videos elsewhere and link to them. Remove files you no longer use and delete old sites you do not need. Operator exceptions apply to a few accounts.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack keeps its own 25 MB upload limit and 2 versions; Enterprise caps stored bytes per owner instead; a small box has no site or account total unless its operator sets one.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §1 L82-92 (200 MB, 1024 MB, SITE_TOTAL_CAP_FROM, after-prune checks, 413 site_total_too_large / account_storage_full, /v1/me file_usage, small box and Hack lines); FEATURES.md §18 L2328 (100 MB default); PARITY rows 'Website file allowances', 'Quotas'. Named account exceptions (chhotabreak, vineetu, jot-transcribe) rendered as 'operator exceptions', no customer names. Not rendered.

features.name: See all your sites
features.line: One list of everything you have published, with its address, its current version number, when it was last deployed, and whether it is live.
features.who: Anyone with more than one site.
features.how: Your sites page lists every site as a card with Open and a Manage menu. Each card shows the live address, the version number, and the last deploy. Taken-down or offline sites say so. Your AI app gets the same list, newest edited first, with each site's file size.
features.example: An agency with thirty client sites opens one page to see which were deployed this week and which still carry last month's version.
features.where: Your sites page, with every button. The main dashboard lists the same sites with a Manage link back there.
features.limits: Your own sites only. A search box appears once you have 10 or more sites; see Find sites by description.
features.evidence: features.html #site-list; FEATURES.md §1 Pages row (showcase.html cards, search from 10 sites) and Routes row (GET /v1/sites newest edited first, file_bytes). Contradiction: the current page says 'there is no search or filter'; FEATURES.md documents search from 10 sites and ?query= filters since 2026-10-23, so FEATURES.md wins. Not rendered.

features.name: Find sites by description
features.line: Search your own sites by words from their pages or by date, so "the one with the pricing table" turns up without knowing its name.
features.who: Anyone with enough sites that names alone stop helping, and every AI app asked to find "my site about X".
features.how: At each deploy Simple Host captures a short summary of the home page: its title, meta description, first headings, and up to 300 bytes of text. Your AI app's site list and the search box on your sites page match words against that summary and the name, and can filter by created or updated date, order by name or date, and page through results.
features.example: A consultant asks "open my site about the Lisbon workshop" and the app finds it by the heading on its home page.
features.where: The search box on your sites page (shown from 10 sites), or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Plain word matching on the home page's summary, your own sites only. The summary is taken from the home page, so words that appear only on other pages are not matched.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (GET /v1/sites ?query=, date filters, ?order=, paging, compact content summary); Pages row (search from 10 sites); PARITY row 'Find sites by description' (summary fields, same on Enterprise 2026-10-24). Hack and small box: not stated, same binary. Not rendered.

features.name: Your 4 latest versions
features.line: Simple Host keeps your live version and 3 to roll back to, numbered and dated, and an older live version always stays.
features.who: Anyone who has ever published something worse than what they had.
features.how: Every publish makes a new numbered version with a timestamp. The newest 4 are kept, counting versions stored but not yet live; the live version is never pruned even when it is older. The version list shows the newest three and the live one, with Show all for the rest. The operator decides who can change the count; on simple-host.app the count is fixed, and asking for a different one answers "Simple Host keeps your 4 latest versions".
features.example: A product team publishes a landing-page redesign on Monday and still has Friday's version to compare against.
features.where: Versions under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Versions carry a number and a timestamp only; there is no note or label on them. Kept versions count toward the site's and the account's file allowance. Deploy-only keys cannot change the count.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack keeps 2 versions, Enterprise keeps 5, and a small box keeps every version unless its operator sets a count, which anyone there may also set per site.
features.evidence: features.html #site-versions and the Managing sites lede ('Simple Host keeps your 4 latest versions; operator exceptions apply. Self-hosted instances choose their own retention'); FEATURES.md §1 L84 (4 versions, 403 keep_versions_fixed text), L90 (small box anyone can set, KEEP_VERSIONS 0 = all; Hack 2), Routes row (keep-versions not for deploy-only keys), Pages row (newest three and the live one, Show all); PARITY row 'Versions kept per site' (Enterprise 5). Not rendered.

features.name: Put an earlier version back
features.line: Pick any kept version and make it the live one again; the switch is immediate.
features.who: Anyone who broke a live page a minute ago and wants it back now.
features.how: Choose a version in the list and make it live. Visitors see it at once at the same address. A version stored for preview but never published is made live the same way.
features.example: A shop's agent publishes a new checkout page that hides the Buy button; the owner puts yesterday's version back while the fix is made.
features.where: Make live in the version list under Versions, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: This changes the pages only. Data your visitors saved is not rolled back: it is not part of a version. Only kept versions can be put back.
features.evidence: features.html #site-rollback; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (PUT /v1/sites/{sitename}/active-version also makes a stored version live) and preview prose ('Make live' is the rollback); PARITY row 'Sites: deploy, versions, rollback, delete'. Not rendered.

features.name: Look before it goes live
features.line: Store a change without publishing it, then open a preview link that shows that version exactly as visitors would see it.
features.who: Anyone whose agent is about to redesign a site people are already using.
features.how: Ask your AI app to publish without making it live. The version is stored and you get a preview link. Any kept version, live or not, can be previewed the same way from the version list. The preview is served on the site's own address, is hidden from search engines, and refuses saves. When you are happy, Make live switches visitors to it.
features.example: A law firm's agent redesigns the home page; the partners open the preview link, ask for two changes, and only then make it live.
features.where: Preview and Make live in the version list under Versions, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: A preview link is yours for one hour, and anyone who has it can open it in that hour. Nothing you do in a preview is saved, so forms there do not submit. A site with no address of its own yet cannot mint a preview link.
features.editions_note: Enterprise preview links open only for the owner or a team member.
features.evidence: features.html #site-preview; FEATURES.md §1 preview prose (publish=false, hour-long bearer link, noindex, saves refused, 409 preview_unavailable with no own address); PARITY row 'Look before it goes live' (Enterprise owner/team only). Hack: preview_version tool exists; the §10 note that 'preview remains unavailable on Hack' refers to the MCP Apps screen. Not rendered.

features.name: Drafts as versions
features.line: Keep several unpublished drafts of one site, each marked with who made it, and discard the ones you will not use.
features.who: Anyone whose agent prepares a few versions of a page before one is chosen: a quote, a proposal, a redesign.
features.how: Publish without making it live, and name the author with the deploy. The version list shows who made each draft and can show only the drafts that have never been live. Make the chosen one live from the list; discard the others and they are gone for good. Versions that have been live are kept by the normal retention rule and cannot be discarded by hand.
features.example: A travel agency keeps one site per quote. Two staff each store a draft of the itinerary; the manager previews both, makes one live, and discards the other.
features.where: Versions under Manage on your sites page (the author beside each draft, Discard on drafts not live yet), or ask your AI app.
features.limits: An author name is at most 80 characters. Discarding is final and applies only to versions that were never live; a deploy-only key or a Simple Hack team key cannot discard.
features.editions_note: On Simple Hack the version list and authors work the same way; team keys cannot discard.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §1 'Drafts as versions' (author on deploys, ?pending=1, DELETE .../versions/{version}, discard_version); PARITY row 'Drafts as versions' (Enterprise: not ported).

features.name: Rename a site
features.line: Give a site a new name without republishing it; its versions and its saved data come with it.
features.who: Anyone who picked a throwaway name and then kept the site.
features.how: Choose Rename and type the new name, or ask your AI app. The site keeps its versions, saved data, and storage. Its address changes with the name.
features.example: A founder published a pitch as `draft-3`, closed the round, and renamed it `investors` before sending the link out.
features.where: Rename under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: The new name must be free and follow the same rules as a new site's name. The old name keeps forwarding to the new address until you create a new site with the old name, which then takes it.
features.evidence: features.html #site-rename; FEATURES.md §1 rename prose (old name 302s until reused); PARITY row 'Site rename'. The redirect is kept to one clause because addresses and legacy redirects belong to another area. Not rendered.

features.name: Delete a site
features.line: Takes the site offline at once, with every version and its saved visitor data, and keeps it in Recently deleted for 7 days.
features.who: Anyone clearing out experiments.
features.how: Choose Delete and a dialog names what goes with it: how many list entries and whether saved data are included. The site goes offline immediately and moves to Recently deleted, which keeps it for 7 days; Restore brings it back whole. Download is in the same menu if you want a copy first.
features.example: An agency closes a finished campaign site after taking a download for the client's records.
features.where: Delete under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: After **7 days** it is gone for good, saved data included. Until then its name stays yours and the site still counts toward your site quota and file allowance. A site taken down by the operator cannot be deleted until the operator acts. Deleting your whole account is immediate.
features.editions_note: Enterprise keeps a deleted site for 30 days.
features.evidence: features.html #site-delete (Recently deleted and Restore split into #publish-recently-deleted; the Who clause 'anyone who deleted the wrong one' moved there); FEATURES.md §1 delete prose (7 days, refused while taken down, account delete immediate) and Limits row (Recently deleted counts toward the cap); PARITY row 'Recently deleted' (Enterprise 30 days). Not rendered.

features.name: Recently deleted
features.line: A deleted site stays in Recently deleted for 7 days, and Restore brings it back exactly as it was, name and data included.
features.who: Anyone who deleted the wrong one.
features.how: Recently deleted on your sites page lists every site deleted in the last 7 days. Restore puts it back whole: its name, versions, saved data, lists, and any claimed name. Your AI app can list and restore them too. After 7 days it is removed for good by an hourly sweep.
features.example: A consultant deletes a client portal by mistake on Friday and restores it on Monday with every entry still there.
features.where: Recently deleted on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: After **7 days** it is gone for good. A site in Recently deleted still counts toward your site quota and file allowance. Its old name does not forward while it is deleted.
features.editions_note: Enterprise keeps deleted sites for 30 days, and a team member or admin may restore as well as the owner.
features.evidence: features.html #site-delete (Recently deleted and Restore facts); FEATURES.md §1 delete prose (7 days, restore brings it back whole, hourly purge, name, saved data, collections and claimed names kept, a deleted site's old names skipped), Routes row (GET /v1/me/deleted-sites, POST .../restore), MCP row (list_deleted_sites, restore_site); PARITY row 'Recently deleted' (Enterprise 30 days, owner, team member or admin). Hack: list_deleted_sites and restore_site exist on Hack. Not rendered.

features.name: Take a site offline
features.line: Every address of the site shows "This site is offline" and visitors can no longer save anything, while nothing is deleted.
features.who: Anyone whose event is over, or whose form must stop taking entries today.
features.how: Choose Take offline, or ask your AI app. Every address answers a plain "This site is offline" page, visitor saves and visitor sign-in are refused, and the site leaves your public showcase. Its pages, versions, and saved data stay exactly as they are. Put back online reverses it whenever you like.
features.example: A conference closes its speaker application form the day the deadline passes and puts the site back online with the programme a week later.
features.where: Take offline and Put back online under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: It is offline for everyone at once. You and your agent can still update it and read its data while it is offline. The offline page is hidden from search engines. An operator take-down overrides the switch.
features.editions_note: Enterprise has no offline switch; its only-me access level does the same job, with visitors seeing the sign-in gate and the owner still opening the site.
features.evidence: features.html #site-offline; FEATURES.md §1 offline prose (503, noindex, 403 site_offline, leaves the person page, owner keeps deploying, take-down wins); PARITY row 'Take a site offline' (Enterprise only-me access level). Hack: set_site_offline exists on Hack. Not rendered.

features.name: Download a site
features.line: One file with every page of the live version, the site's saved data, and everything its lists hold, to keep or take elsewhere.
features.who: Anyone about to delete a site, make a big change, or leave.
features.how: Choose Download on your sites page and a `.tar.gz` archive is prepared with the live files, the saved data, and the list entries with their ids, dates, and who submitted them. Your AI app gets a 10-minute download link to the same archive.
features.example: A client ends an engagement and the agency hands over the download, pages and form entries together, so nothing is lost when the site is deleted.
features.where: Download under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: A `.tar.gz` archive, as it is at that moment. There is no way to upload it back in one step; your agent can republish the pages from it. A download link from your AI app expires after 10 minutes and stops working if the site is deleted or renamed in between.
features.editions_note: The Enterprise archive is a zip that also carries versions and uploaded files, through a single-use link.
features.evidence: features.html #site-download; FEATURES.md §1 Routes row (export.tar.gz with collections.json id, created_at, submitted_by; 10-minute export link; 404 export_link_invalid when expired, deleted or changed); PARITY row 'Site export with saved data'. Hack: export_site exists on Hack. Not rendered.

features.name: Public or unlisted
features.line: A public site is listed on your showcase page; an unlisted one is hidden there and from search engines, but opens for anyone with the link.
features.who: Anyone with drafts, client work, or personal pages they do not want on a public list.
features.how: New sites start unlisted. Make public lists the site on your showcase page and lets search engines index it. Make unlisted takes it off the showcase and asks search engines to stay away, unless the site has its own domain or name, which is read as a wish to be found.
features.example: A designer keeps client drafts unlisted while they are reviewed and makes the finished portfolio pieces public.
features.where: Make unlisted and Make public under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Unlisted is not private; anyone with the link can open it. Search engines are asked not to index it, and a site that ships its own robots.txt keeps that file. An unlisted site with its own domain or name is not hidden from search engines.
features.editions_note: Enterprise decides who can open a site with access levels instead of a public or unlisted switch.
features.evidence: features.html #site-visibility (Where said 'on your sites page only'; FEATURES.md lists set_visibility and PUT /v1/sites/{sitename}/visibility, so the AI app can do it too, FEATURES.md wins); FEATURES.md §1 lead (unlisted default, X-Robots-Tag, robots.txt, own domain or name exempt); PARITY row 'Who can open a site' for Enterprise access levels. Hack: set_visibility exists; not stated for Hack showcase. Not rendered.

features.name: A proper "page not found"
features.line: A mistyped address on a site gets a clean, branded page with a way back, instead of a raw server error.
features.who: Your visitors, on their worst moment.
features.how: When a visitor asks for a page the site does not have, the web server hands the request to Simple Host, which answers a branded not-found page in the site's theme with a link back. The old name of a renamed site forwards instead of showing it.
features.example: A customer follows a stale link to a product page that was renamed and lands on a clear page with a way back to the shop.

features.name: Move a WordPress site
features.line: Upload the export of a WordPress site you own and Simple Host turns it into static pages at the same permalinks, with photos and menus.
features.who: Someone moving a WordPress or Squarespace site they own, with only a chat app.
features.how: Ask your AI app to start a WordPress import for a site name. It gives you a one-time page where you upload the export: the WXR `.xml` file, WordPress.com's `.zip` of XML files, and the media library as a `.tar`, `.zip`, or `.tar.gz` of `wp-content/uploads`. features.line: A site unvisited and unchanged for 90 days gets its owner a Keep link by email; 30 days later with nothing done it is deleted.

areas.title: Domains and addresses
areas.line: Where a site answers: its own address from the first minute, a short free name, your own domain, or one wildcard for every site you own.

features.name: Every site gets a public address
features.line: The moment a site exists it has a working web address you can send to anyone, with HTTPS already on.
features.who: Everyone. This is the point of the service.
features.how: Every site gets its own address, `https://<site>.<handle>.simple-host.app/`. Files are served at the root, and visitor sign-in, per-person saves, and private collections are bound to that host, so a sign-in covers that one site. On a brand-new account the address can be `https://<handle>.simple-host.app/<site>/` for the first few minutes, until its certificate is ready; the address shown is always the one that works. For a nicer address, take a free `<name>.simple-host.app` or connect your own domain.
features.example: A consultancy publishes a client proposal and sends the link the same hour; the client opens it over HTTPS with nothing to set up.
features.where: Under each site's name on your sites page, with its live version and when it was last deployed. A site with its own live domain shows that domain.
features.limits: simple-host.app is the only address served and handed out by the hosted service; pages, API examples, connector text, and skills all use `.app`. Old links on another base redirect to the matching `.app` address with path and query kept. A site's `/v1/` path is reserved for the API of that one site.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack team sites live on the event's hosts; a small box without per-site hosts serves every site by path on one shared address.

features.name: Your handle is an address too
features.line: Your handle has its own host, https://<handle>.simple-host.app/, which lists your public sites or opens the site you chose as home.
features.who: Anyone who wants one link for all their work, or a short address to put on a card.
features.how: Every handle is a host. By default `https://<handle>.simple-host.app/` shows your public showcase. You can pick one of your sites as your home page instead (see Showcase and home page). On a brand-new account, until your certificate is ready, your sites are reached beneath it as `<handle>.simple-host.app/<site>/`; once it is ready those paths forward to each site's own address.
features.example: A freelance designer prints `https://meera.simple-host.app/` on a business card; it lists her live portfolio, a pricing page, and a client demo.
features.where: Shown on your sites page under Your address. Your AI app reports it as your person page.
features.limits: Only public sites are listed. A renamed handle keeps the old one forwarding to the new one. Handles that read as Simple Host or a sensitive function are reserved.
features.editions_note: Enterprise has an owner index page that needs company sign-in; a small box without per-site hosts serves the person page by path; Simple Hack has no personal sites.

features.name: Your own address is on its way
features.line: Each person gets a certificate for *.<handle>.simple-host.app on their first site, and the service tells you while it is still queued.
features.who: New accounts in their first minutes, and anyone wondering why a site still shows the path form of its address.
features.how: The certificate is requested automatically when you publish your first site and is usually ready within about 10 minutes. Until then your sites keep the `<handle>.simple-host.app/<site>/` form, and every address handed out is whichever one is live. While it is not ready, your sites page shows a note at the top, and your AI app sees the state too: waiting (queued, with a rough time from the queue) or failing (retried after the issuer's six-hour wait). When the address switches, the note also says that visitors' sign-ins and anything a page kept in the visitor's browser start fresh on the new address.
features.example: A new account publishes a landing page for a product launch at 9:00 and shares the path-form link; by 9:10 the site answers at its own address and the old link forwards.
features.where: A note at the top of your sites page while it is on its way; each site's card shows the address that currently works.
features.limits: Brand-new accounts may queue behind the issuer's weekly and daily caps, and the note shows what was issued in the last week against those caps. A request that stays unready is retried on its own; nothing for you to press. Browser-kept data and sign-ins do not carry over to the new address.
features.editions_note: Enterprise issues per-owner certificates inside the cluster and shows the waiting state to admins only; a small box uses one shared address and needs no per-person certificate.

features.name: Old addresses still work
features.line: Links in the older address styles forward to the site's own address, so anything you already shared keeps opening.
features.who: Anyone who published before the address format changed.
features.how: Old `<handle>.simple-host.app/<site>/` and `sites.simple-host.app/<handle>/<site>/` links redirect to the site's own address, with the path and query kept. A renamed site's old name keeps redirecting on all three forms until a new site takes that name. A free name a site let go stays with it and redirects to its current address, or says "This site was removed" once the site is gone.
features.example: A bakery's menu link printed on flyers last spring as `sites.simple-host.app/anna/menu/` still lands on the menu at its current address.
features.where: Nothing to do: the old link forwards on its own.
features.limits: Visitors land on the new address, so that is what they will see in the address bar and copy from then on. What a page kept in the visitor's browser starts fresh there; what the site saved on the server moves with it.
features.editions_note: The older address forms existed on simple-host.app only; a renamed site's old name redirects on every edition.

features.name: A free <name>.simple-host.app
features.line: Take a short free address such as my-shop.simple-host.app for a site; it is live at once, with HTTPS and no registrar.
features.who: Anyone who wants a short link to print or say out loud.
features.how: Pick a name and it is verified at once, first come first served. The site's longer address redirects to it, and sign-in and saved data move with it. If you later switch names, disconnect, or delete the site, the old name stays with that site and keeps redirecting to its current address.
features.example: A yoga studio takes `riverside-yoga.simple-host.app` for its class schedule and reads it out at the end of each class.
features.where: Domain under Manage on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: One name per site, first come first served. Lower-case letters, numbers, and dashes. Names that read as Simple Host or a sensitive function (support, admin, billing, login, and similar) are reserved. A released name cannot be taken by another site; it stays with the site that had it.

features.name: Point your own domain at a site
features.line: Attach a domain you own, a subdomain or the bare domain, to one site; it is then served only there and its old address redirects.
features.who: Anyone with a brand, a business or a domain already bought.
features.how: Attach a domain you own, a subdomain like `recipes.yourbrand.com` or the bare domain itself, to one of your sites. You add two DNS records at your registrar; the service checks them about every two minutes and requests the certificate on its own once both are seen. Once connected, the site is served only on your domain: its `<site>.<handle>.simple-host.app` address redirects there, and visitors sign in and save there. Connecting a new domain to a site that already has one keeps the current address serving until the new one is live with its certificate; then the old one redirects.
features.example: An architecture practice connects `studio.hallam.co` to its project showcase, so nothing in the address mentions a hosting service.
features.where: Connect domain under Manage on your sites page. Your agent can also do it, and there is a skill for exactly this.
features.limits: One domain per site. A binding is provisional until its TXT ownership record proves it: another site can take an unproven one over, and it lapses after 24 hours if DNS never pointed here (7 days in any case). A proven domain is exclusive (`409 domain_taken`). A name another site on this server already serves cannot be connected. Each account may ask for at most 5 new domain certificates a day; the sixth waits. Sites that are taken down, and suspended accounts, get no domain checks. [[hosted]]`simple-hack.app` and the service's own zones cannot be connected.[[/hosted]]

features.name: You are told the exact records to add
features.line: Connecting hands back the two DNS records for your registrar: one that points the domain here and a TXT record that proves it is yours.
features.who: Whoever has the login to the domain registrar; often not the person building the site.
features.how: Connecting returns both records: a CNAME for a subdomain or an A record for a bare domain, and a TXT record at `_simple-host.<your domain>` holding the site's token. Keep the TXT record in place; the domain counts as verified only while it matches and the site answers over HTTPS. Your agent can repeat the records any time, and Check again re-proves them on the spot.
features.example: The site is built by a marketing lead, but the domain lives with the company's IT person; the lead forwards the two records and IT pastes them in.
features.where: Shown when you connect, and repeatable by your agent afterwards.
features.limits: Adding it at the registrar is yours to do, and changes can take from minutes to a few hours to spread. Domains verified before 27 September 2026 keep working without the TXT record while they stay verified. Check again allows 3 checks at once per account, then one every 30 seconds.

features.name: HTTPS on your domain
features.line: A connected domain is served over HTTPS with a valid certificate, requested on its own once your records are in place.
features.who: Everyone: a browser warning on your own domain is worse than no domain.
features.how: The certificate is issued automatically once your domain points here and its ownership record (a TXT record at `_simple-host.<your domain>`) is in place, usually within minutes. The issuer re-checks the TXT record and that the domain still points at your site before issuing. Until then your site keeps its current address. `www` and the bare domain can both work on one certificate.
features.example: A law firm moves its client intake page to `intake.marsh-law.com`; the padlock is there before anyone is sent the link.
features.where: Nothing to press.
features.limits: At most 5 new domain certificates per account per day; the sixth waits and the status says so. A failed request is retried after 6 hours; DNS and TXT problems are retried after 15 minutes. A domain that points here but never proves itself is released after 7 days, and the site's earlier address comes back.
features.editions_note: Follows custom domains: on a small box the server's own web front issues the certificate on demand.

features.name: The connection badge
features.line: Your sites page shows the domain you attached with its status, the records still to add, the last check's result, and Check again.
features.who: Anyone checking whether the connection worked.
features.how: Until the domain is live, Domain shows the two DNS records to add, what the last check found, when an unproven connection lapses, the certificate's state, and Check again. For www and the bare domain it also shows the partner's record and whether it was set up. Your agent reads the same status.
features.example: A shop owner adds the records on Friday evening, sees pending with "TXT record not found", fixes a typo, presses Check again, and sees active.
features.where: Next to the site's name on your sites page, and under Domain.
features.limits: Re-checked about every two minutes: pending until the domain resolves here and answers over HTTPS, then active (or error, with the reason). An active verdict is re-proved every hour. Opening the domain is still the surest test.
features.editions_note: Follows custom domains.

features.name: A domain that stops pointing here is let go
features.line: A connected domain that keeps failing its checks is emailed about and then disconnected, so the site's own address serves again.
features.who: Anyone who let a domain expire, moved DNS elsewhere, or inherited a site whose domain no longer points here.
features.how: If it fails every check for a day, the owner is emailed with the last error. After three days the domain is disconnected and released completely: the binding, the server entry, and the certificate go, the site's own `<site>.<handle>.simple-host.app` address serves again, and the domain can be connected afresh with the TXT proof. The earlier address kept while a new domain is pending is checked the same way and let go after three days of failing.
features.example: An agency hands a client site back and the client repoints the domain to another host; three days later the site is back on its Simple Host address and the agency's dashboard shows no domain.
features.where: The email arrives at your account address; the Domain panel shows the last error and when the domain will be released.
features.limits: While the issuer is still letting go of a released domain, connecting it again answers "domain releasing"; try again shortly. A free name the site lets go is not released; it stays with the site and redirects.

features.name: Disconnect a domain
features.line: Detaches the domain and stops serving your site from it, so the site's own address serves again and the domain is free for another site.
features.who: Anyone moving a domain to a different site, or retiring one.
features.how: Detaches the domain and stops serving your site from it, freeing the domain to be used on another site. The site's `<site>.<handle>.simple-host.app` address stops redirecting and serves the site again, with sign-in and saving there, and links people kept to the domain stop working. Your agent confirms with you first, then removes exactly the domain you name.

features.where: Disconnect under Domain in the site's Manage menu on your sites page.

features.line: Connect brand.com and www.brand.com answers too (or the other way round); the partner redirects to the name you chose, on one certificate.
features.who: Anyone whose visitors type the domain either way.

features.where: Offered when you connect a domain; the records to add are shown with the rest.
features.limits: The partner only redirects; it never serves a second copy of the site. It is set up only if it points here, nothing else on this server answers it, and it is not connected to a site of its own. A partner that another site has bound, in any account, is neither offered nor asked for. A partner that later becomes a site of its own is taken off the redirect first.

features.name: One wildcard for every site you own
features.line: Connect *.<suffix> once and every site of your account answers at <label>.<suffix>, including sites you make later.
features.who: Agencies and businesses that make many sites under one brand: a quote per client, a page per property, a portal per customer.

Every site named `<label>` then answers at `<label>.trips.example.com`, with no per-site step. An optional site prefix maps `voucher-meera` to `meera.voucher.example.com`. A site with its own custom domain or free name keeps that as its main address; the same account may put a custom domain under its own family.

areas.title: Storage and saved data
areas.line: Where a site keeps what visitors send and what the owner changes from chat, with rules for who may read, add, edit, and delete.

features.name: Three kinds of site storage
features.line: Every site gets key-value namespaces, its own SQLite database, and file buckets, so pages can save and read without a server.
features.who: Anyone whose site takes bookings, orders, form entries, uploads, or content the owner changes from chat.
features.how: The owner's AI app creates a storage resource on the site and gives it a name: a key-value namespace for settings and small documents, a SQLite database with tables for records, or a file bucket for uploads. Each resource carries an access preset that says who may read, add, edit, and delete. Pages on the site read and write through `auth.js`; the owner's app reads and writes everything through the connector. The three kinds are opt-in and start owner-only, and a resource can inherit the site's passcode. Saves can also tell the owner's agent through a webhook, covered under Notifications.
features.example: A restaurant keeps its menu and prices in a public key-value namespace, so the owner says "raise the lunch special to 14" in chat and the page shows it on the next load.
features.where: Ask your AI app. The Storage panel beneath each site on your sites page lists every resource, its policy, and how much space it uses.

features.name: Access presets: who may read, add, edit, and delete
features.line: Each namespace, table, and bucket has four actions, and a preset names who may do each, so nobody writes access rules by hand.
features.who: Anyone deciding what visitors may see and change on a site: a form only the owner reads, records each person sees alone, a wall anyone reads.
features.how: Four actions (read, add, edit, delete), each set to nobody, owner, own (the signed-in person who added the entry), signed-in, or anyone. Eight presets name the common settings. `public`: anyone reads, the owner changes. `inbox`: anyone adds, only the owner reads and changes. `wall`: anyone reads, signed-in people add and delete their own, the owner edits. `records`: each signed-in person reads their own, the owner reads and changes all. `personal`: each signed-in person reads, edits, and deletes their own. `board`: signed-in people read, add, and edit, the owner deletes. `private` (the default): owner only. `comments`: anyone reads, anyone adds after a spam check, the owner edits and deletes. A SQLite database takes a preset per table with the database's own as the default, and a single action can be overridden. The server refuses four unsafe settings when saved: anyone may edit or delete, add set to own, own anywhere with add set to anyone, and edit or delete wider than read.
features.example: A tutoring business sets its `requests` table to `inbox` so parents send a request without signing in and only the owner reads them, and its `homework` table to `records` so each student sees only their own submissions.
features.where: Your AI app sets the preset when it builds the page. The Storage panel beneath each site on your sites page shows each resource's policy with the choices Anyone can add, Only signed-in visitors can add, Each person sees only their own, and Only you.
features.limits: 161 of the 625 possible settings are allowed. Resources saved before presets keep their older rules until the owner saves a policy. Visitors never send SQL on a database with a preset; pages use the server's row routes.
features.editions_note: On Simple Hack the owner is the team until its submission deadline, or the organisers until the event ends; Enterprise has the same presets and rules on its own engine, where anonymous visitors to a network-approved site read anyone data and never write.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §23 'Access presets' paragraph; PARITY rows 'Storage access presets (2026-10-10)' and 'Comments preset'. Dashboard choice wording from §23 visitor-routes paragraph.

features.name: Pages read and write table rows without SQL
features.line: A page lists, adds, edits, and deletes rows through fixed routes the server builds, so a visitor can never run a query of their own.
features.who: Anyone whose site shows records to visitors: orders, bookings, requests, entries in a directory.
features.how: A page asks for rows with up to three equality filters plus an order, a direction, a limit, and a cursor for the next page. It adds a row by sending column values. The server validates the table and columns against the real schema, stamps `id`, `visitor_id`, `created_at`, and `updated_at`, and ignores any id or time the page sends. Edits and deletes under own touch only the caller's row; another person's row answers not found. Visitors see a `mine` mark on each entry instead of other people's ids. A linked row must point at a parent the visitor may read, and a change that would write another table through a trigger or cascade is refused. Owner tools still run full SQL, within a time limit.
features.example: A clinic's booking page lists `appointments` where the status is open, ordered by date, and shows each patient only their own rows.
features.where: Your page's own code through `auth.js`. Your AI app runs the owner's queries and schema changes.
features.limits: 100 rows per page by default, at most 500. At most 100 columns on a visitor route. Use `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` so the server assigns ids. A duplicate in a unique column answers a generic conflict, so use opaque ids rather than emails as unique keys. Visitor queries stop after 1 second and visitor writes after 2 seconds; owner operations get 5 seconds.
features.editions_note: Enterprise builds the same row routes over declared tables on Postgres.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §23 'Access presets' paragraph (row routes, filters, stamps) and the SQLite paragraphs (defaults 100/500, 100 columns, row_conflict, timeouts); PARITY row 'Storage access presets' (visitors never send SQL).

features.where: No screen. Ask your agent to allow the address.
features.limits: Up to 20 addresses per site, and you have to name each one exactly.

features.name: Save what a form collects
features.line: Each submission is added to a named list, one row per entry, separate from the shared box so it can grow well past it.
features.who: Anyone with a form: an event page, a waitlist, a contact form, a survey.
features.how: A collection is where form entries go: RSVPs, signups, orders, messages. Adding stays fast no matter how long the list gets. Visitors append; in Submissions each visitor can see, change, and withdraw their own, and on a Shared board anyone signed in edits items. You can delete any entry, or empty the whole list, from your page or through your agent. A retried save with the same key is stored once for a signed-in writer.
features.example: A language school's older enrolment form adds each application to an `applications` list that the office reviews every morning.
features.where: Your page's own code saves to it.
features.limits: Up to 64 KB per entry (each new entry is at most 16 KB in declared Submissions, and a declared Submissions name holds at most 10,000 live entries). Entries in a public list cannot be edited. Entries added without the owner's key are limited to 30 a minute per address.

features.name: Read the entries back on the page
features.line: A page reads its own entries, newest first, so a sign-up list or a public wall can show what has come in.
features.who: Anyone who wants the results visible rather than hidden behind a login.
features.how: The page asks for the list and gets the newest entries first, a page at a time, with a cursor for the next page. Who sent each entry is left out of every read but the owner's.
features.example: A running club's older results page lists the finishers members entered, newest first.

features.limits: 200 entries at a time maximum, 50 by default. Anything a page can read, a visitor can read.

features.name: See what a site has collected
features.line: Every list on a site, public or private, with its entry count, when the last one arrived, and a table of the entries themselves.
features.who: You, checking whether anyone actually filled the form in, or cleaning up after spam.
features.how: Each list shows a public or private badge, View items, a spreadsheet, and a More menu with the privacy switch, Settings, History, and Recently deleted. You can delete any entry (spam in a comment list, a test entry), correct an entry in a private list, or clear a whole list after typing its name. The owner's view adds a sent by column. Your agent can do the same.
features.example: A dentist checks the older appointment-request list on Monday, deletes two spam entries, and corrects a typo in a patient's phone number.
features.where: Lists beneath the site on your sites page. Your agent can do the same.

features.name: Download everything as a spreadsheet
features.line: One button gives you the whole collection as a CSV file you can open in any spreadsheet.
features.who: Anyone who has to actually use the entries: a sign-up list to check off, a mailing list to import.
features.how: Press Download spreadsheet next to the list and a CSV of every live entry arrives. The owner's export adds a last column with who sent each entry. Cells that look like formulas are made safe for spreadsheet programs.
features.example: A conference organiser downloads the older speaker-application list and sorts it by track in a spreadsheet.
features.where: Download spreadsheet next to the list on your sites page.
features.limits: A snapshot at the moment you press it. No filtering or date range; you get the whole list.

features.name: Private collections
features.line: A collection can be made private: only signed-in visitors submit, you read them all, and each visitor sees and changes only their own.
features.who: Anyone collecting personal details: orders, RSVPs, sign-ups.
features.how: Only signed-in visitors can submit, from the site's own address, never by API key. Each entry is stamped with the visitor's verified email and the time. You read them all and may edit them; each visitor sees, changes, and withdraws only their own. A list made public again keeps its submitters' emails private: who sent what is shown to the owner alone.
features.example: A physiotherapist's older intake form stores each patient's details in a private collection that only she reads.
features.where: Make private next to the list on your sites page, or choose Submissions under the list's Settings, or ask your agent. Visitors submit on the site's own address; you read the entries on your sites page, on an owner page on the site, or as a CSV.
features.limits: Making a private collection public again shows everything already in it, so the page and your agent ask first. The site needs an address of its own.

features.name: Four kinds of saved data
features.line: Each data name is one kind, and the kind decides who reads and who changes what: Page info, Submissions, Personal, or Shared board.
features.who: Anyone building a form, a menu, a habit tracker, or a group list without writing access rules.
features.how: Page info: you write, everyone reads. Submissions: visitors send; private to you by default, and public only without who sent them; each visitor lists, changes, and withdraws their own, and brings back what they withdrew for 10 minutes; a name can take one entry per person. Personal: one private record per signed-in visitor that follows them to any device; only that visitor reads or writes it, and you see how many people have a record and the total size from 3 people up. Shared board: a list a group edits item by item with a version check, and only you empty it. A name nobody declared is Shared, as before: anyone reads it and signed-in visitors save to it.
features.example: A music teacher's older site keeps the term dates as Page info, lesson requests as Submissions, and each student's practice log as a Personal record.
features.where: Your AI app declares each name when it builds the site; you see and change the kind under Settings next to each name on your sites page.
features.limits: A Page info document is at most 1 MB, and a site declares at most 20 Page info names. Each new entry is at most 16 KB, a name holds at most 10,000 live entries, and a site declares at most 50 Submissions names. A personal record is at most 64 KB, and a name holds records for at most 1,000 people. A board item is at most 16 KB, and a board holds at most 2,000 live items. A site declares at most 20 Personal names, and declares at most 20 Shared board names. All but Page info need the site on an address of its own. A site's own pages can read a visitor's Personal record, so it is as private as the site's pages are trustworthy.

features.name: Who may save here, and Block
features.line: Choose whether anyone who signs in may save on a site, or only listed emails and whole domains, and block one person with a click.
features.who: Anyone whose form is for a club, a class, or a company, and anyone dealing with a troublemaker.
features.how: A site setting that covers every visitor write on the site: page data, lists, and Submissions. Anyone who signs in may save (the default), or only listed emails and whole `@domains`. Either way a block list applies, filled from Block next to any entry. A block and the one-per-person rule match the person's address with a `+tag` dropped, and Block by entry uses only the address the server stamped.

features.name: Email me when something arrives
features.line: New Submissions can email you once a day, soon after each arrives, or not at all, and every email has a link that stops them.
features.who: Anyone taking orders, RSVPs, or sign-ups who will not check the page every day.
features.how: Once a day is the default for private Submissions and off is the default for public ones. The email goes to the site owner's address with a stop link that opens a confirmation page. Each email is sent once even across servers, and an entry saved while a digest was being sent goes into the next one.
features.example: A florist with an older order form gets one email each morning saying how many orders came in overnight.
features.where: Email me under the name's Settings on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Soon after they arrive means at most one email per name every 10 minutes, counting what came in. The email carries counts and the list's name, not the entries. A failed send is not retried.

features.name: History, Restore, and Delete for good
features.line: Every change to saved data is kept for 30 days with who made it, so you can undo one change, put a document back, or restore entries.
features.who: Anyone whose page data was overwritten, or who deleted the wrong entry.
features.how: Every write to the shared document and every edit, delete, clear, and restore in a list is recorded with who made it (their account and the address they signed in with) and when. Open History to see the document before any change, undo one change, or restore a version; a restore is itself a change. Open Recently deleted to bring back entries one by one or all at once. On a Shared board, Restore all names a window from 15 minutes to 30 days so it brings back what went since then, never what people deleted on purpose before. Delete forever removes an entry and its history at once, for a person who asks to be erased or a flood of spam, and Clear history removes every earlier version of a site's data after you type the site's name. Each visitor also has a 30-day history of their own Personal record.
features.example: A bakery's older menu document is overwritten by mistake; the owner opens History, views Friday's version, and restores it.
features.where: History and Recently deleted under the site's data on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Every change is kept for 30 days: the owner restores any of it. A deleted entry stays in Recently deleted for **30 days**, then is gone for good. Past 20 MB of history per site, the oldest versions are thinned, always keeping each day's first full copy and the record of who deleted what. Live entries are never touched by Delete forever, and Recently deleted does not count toward the site's cap.
features.editions_note: Enterprise keeps the last 20 writes of a site's saved document and the owner or team restores one; there is no Recently deleted for lists.
