areas.title: Sign-in and access
areas.line: How owners and visitors sign in, the keys an AI agent uses, and who may open a site.

features.name: Sign in with an emailed code
features.line: Type your email, get a six-digit code, type it back. No password, and your first code creates the account.
features.who: Anyone starting out, and any visitor who needs to sign in to post on a site.
features.how: Enter your email in the sign-in card and press Continue. A six-digit code arrives; paste or type it and the card signs you in as soon as the sixth digit is in. Your first code creates the account, with no separate sign-up step. The same card is used on the home page, on the connector's consent page, on Simple Hack, and on the shared sign-in page a site sends visitors to.
features.example: A consultant publishes a client document from their AI app, then signs in on simple-host.app with a code to see the address and manage the site.
features.where: The sign-in box on the home page.
features.limits: The code expires after **15 minutes** and you get three tries before you have to ask for a new one. Resend is available after 30 seconds. Codes are limited per email address and per IP, so a burst of requests from one place is refused for a while. A server that cannot send email cannot offer codes.
features.editions_note: Enterprise signs people in with the company's identity provider only; a small box needs outgoing email set up, and may turn codes off in favour of company sign-in.
features.evidence: features.html signin-email-code; FEATURES.md §7 L747-749 (6 digits, 15 min, 3 tries), §6 L700-712 (shared card, 30-second resend), §7 Limits row (ipLimiter, emailLimiter); PARITY row 'Owner sign-in and sessions'. Hack: same card per FEATURES.md §6 L704-706.

features.name: Sign in by tapping the link in the email
features.line: The same email carries a link. Tapping it signs you in without typing the code at all.
features.who: Phone users, mostly: it saves copying digits between apps.
features.how: Ask for a code as usual. The email that brings the code also carries a link. Open it in the browser you asked from and you land signed in, with no code to copy. If the link is opened in a different browser, the card says so and offers the code instead.
features.example: A shop owner on their phone taps the link in the email and lands on their sites page without switching between the mail app and the browser.
features.where: The email itself. You land on your sites page already signed in.
features.limits: Same 15-minute expiry, and the link only works once. It signs in the account on the sign-in page it was asked from; a visitor signing in on a site types the code.
features.editions_note: Enterprise has no emailed codes or links; a small box needs outgoing email set up.
features.evidence: features.html signin-magic-link; FEATURES.md §7 L747 ('6 digits + dashboard-only magic link, 15 min, 3 tries'), §6 L699 (reason link_other_browser). The current page says 'You land back on the site'; FEATURES.md says the link is dashboard-only, so the Where text now says the sites page.

features.name: Sign in with Google
features.line: One tap instead of the email round-trip. It is the same account as the email sign-in when the addresses match.
features.who: Site visitors saving something on a site, and owners who would rather not wait for mail.
features.how: Continue with Google is the first button on the sign-in card. Google confirms who you are and you come back signed in. When the Google address matches an account that signs in by email, it is the same account, so you will not end up with two. A page on your site offers the same button through the hosted sign-in helper; that sign-in only ever makes a visitor session, never an account key.
features.example: A visitor booking a table on a restaurant's site taps Continue with Google and the booking is saved under their name without an email round-trip.
features.where: Under the email box on the home page, and on your site, on the site's own address, through the hosted sign-in helper.
features.limits: Google is the provider today on simple-host.app. GitHub is wired but not switched on. Self-hosted installs can add their company's identity provider as another button. Linked Google sign-ins are listed under Sign-in on your sites page with Unlink.
features.editions_note: Enterprise uses the company's identity provider instead; a small box needs its own Google OAuth client set up before the button appears.
features.evidence: features.html signin-google; FEATURES.md §6 L636-639 (Google configured, GitHub wired but unconfigured), §6 L686-690 (Google start on a site host never mints a key), §7 L832 (Unlink); PARITY row 'Owner sign-in and sessions'. 'More providers later' on the current page replaced with the concrete facts (GitHub wired, company OIDC on self-hosted).

features.name: Choose your address at sign-up
features.line: When a sign-in would create a new account, you pick your address first, checked while you type.
features.who: Anyone making their first account, and agents registering one for a person.
features.how: When an emailed code, link, or Google sign-in would create a new account, the card asks "Choose your address" first. It is prefilled with the address you would have been given and checked while you type, so a taken or reserved name is named under the field before you press Continue. Closing the question creates nothing, and the code still works if you come back. An AI agent registering an account can propose an address the same way.
features.example: A freelance designer signs up and types their studio name as the address so every client site lives under studio.simple-host.app from the first publish.
features.where: The sign-in card, the first time a sign-in would create an account.
features.limits: A taken or reserved address is refused without using up your code. The same check runs when you change the address later under Your address.
features.editions_note: Enterprise names come from the company directory; Simple Hack accounts have no personal address to pick.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §7 L784-790; §7 Routes row (choose_handle, suggested_handle, invalid_handle / handle_reserved / handle_taken without using up the code). Not stated for Simple Hack; features.html your-home-page says Simple Hack has no personal sites, so read as no.

features.name: Your handle
features.line: Every account gets a short public name. It is part of every address you publish and the address of your public profile.
features.who: Everyone with an account; it is how visitors tell your sites apart from anyone else's.
features.how: Your handle is the middle of every site address, site.handle.simple-host.app, and the address of your public page at simple-host.app/handle. You pick it at sign-up, or it is made from your email. Your address on your sites page shows it with Change; the new name is checked while you type and confirmed before it is saved, and a refused save names the problem under the field without signing you out.
features.example: An agency changes its handle after a rebrand; every client site's old address redirects to the new one and the agency's public page moves with it.
features.where: In every site address, and at the top of your sites page. Your address on your sites page shows it, with Change.
features.limits: Before you have published anything the handle is free to change. Once you have published, it can change once every 30 days: the old handle is kept as an alias so every old address redirects to the new one, a certificate for the new address is requested, and what your pages kept in visitors' browsers starts fresh.
features.editions_note: On Enterprise a person's name comes from the company directory and an admin renames; Simple Hack has no personal sites.
features.evidence: features.html account-handle; FEATURES.md §7 L788-790 (Your address → Change checks while typing), §7 Routes row PATCH /v1/me (free before publishing, once per 30 days, alias, certificate); PARITY row 'Change a person's address (handle)'. Hack: not stated; read as no (no personal sites).

features.name: A key for your AI agent
features.line: A personal key that lets your coding agent publish and manage sites for you without you being at the keyboard.
features.who: Anyone using a coding agent rather than clicking through screens.
features.how: Each sign-in gives the browser or agent a new key, and the Keys panel lets you mint more by hand. Each key has a name (typed, or where it came from, such as "dashboard sign-in" or "agent sign-in"), its last four characters, and when it was last used. A key is shown once at creation and stored only as a hash, so it can never be shown again. You revoke one at a time, or Sign out everywhere to replace them all.
features.example: A developer mints a key named "laptop agent" and gives it to the coding agent that publishes their product's landing page and changelog.
features.where: The Keys panel on your sites page: create a named key (tick Deploy only for a CI secret: it can publish, roll back and list sites and nothing else), see when each was last used and when it expires, revoke one, or Sign out everywhere.
features.limits: Each sign-in adds a new key, and older keys keep working until revoked. A key unused for 180 days stops working. A key can also be given a fixed expiry when you create it. Keys are stored only as hashes, so a key cannot be shown again later. Treat it like a password. Minting, revoking, and signing out need one of the account's own keys; a connected app cannot do it, and the connector's only account tool, `who_am_i`, is read-only. When a key stops working, the refusal says why: revoked or unknown, expired on its date, or unused too long, each telling you to create a new key.
features.editions_note: Enterprise keys expire after a fixed lifetime, 90 days by default, and warn in the last 14 days.
features.evidence: features.html api-key; FEATURES.md §7 L747-760 (shk_, SHA-256, names, last 4, last_used_at, Keys panel, own key needed), §7 Limits row (50 keys); PARITY rows 'API keys: hashing', 'API keys: list and revoke one', 'Why a key stopped working', 'Account/credential actions and MCP', 'API keys: expiry' (Enterprise 90 days, 14-day warning). Hack: same binary, not stated separately.

features.name: Deploy-only keys and key expiry
features.line: A key for CI that can publish, roll back, and list sites and nothing else, with an expiry you choose or an idle cut-off.
features.who: Anyone putting a Simple Host key in a CI pipeline or a build server.
features.how: Tick Deploy only when you create a key in the Keys panel. That key may create, update, roll back and list sites, read their versions and files, and make preview links. Everything else is refused: deleting or renaming a site, domains, keys, saved data, storage, analytics, account settings, and connecting apps. The same rule applies on the API and through the connector. You can also give any panel-minted key a fixed expiry, from 1 to 3,650 days. The Keys list shows a Deploy only badge, last used, and the expiry or the date the key stops if it stays unused.
features.example: A product team puts a deploy-only key in GitHub Actions so every merge publishes the docs site, while saved data and domains stay out of the pipeline's reach.
features.where: The Keys panel on your sites page, and the deploy-from-CI notes in the website-deploy skill.
features.limits: A key unused for 180 days stops working. The count runs from its last use. Expired keys stay listed, do not count toward the per-account key limit, and are deleted 30 days after they stopped. A deploy key never carries admin powers, even one an admin minted. Treat a deploy key like the site itself: it can ship code that runs when someone views the site.
features.editions_note: Enterprise's CI scope is called `publish` and also writes saved data; its keys have a fixed lifetime (90 days by default) rather than an idle cut-off.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §7 L762-782; PARITY rows 'API keys: scopes', 'API keys: expiry'. Hack: same binary, not stated separately.

features.name: Sign out, or sign out everywhere
features.line: Sign out ends the key this browser holds. Sign out everywhere stops every key, app connection, and site sign-in at once.
features.who: Anyone who lost a laptop, shared a key by mistake or got a sign-in alert they did not expect.
features.how: Sign out in the header deletes the key this browser held and clears what the browser kept, and since 29 October 2026 it also ends the shared sign-in pass that carried you onto sites, and every site session that came from it. Sign out everywhere replaces every key on the account, disconnects every connected app, and ends every sign-in on your sites; the browser you pressed it in gets a fresh key. Each connected app can also be disconnected on its own from the connected-apps list.
features.example: A founder gets a sign-in alert for a browser they do not recognise, presses Sign out everywhere, and reconnects their own AI app with the fresh key.
features.where: Sign out in the header, and Sign out everywhere in the Keys panel on your sites page.
features.limits: Your agents need the new key afterwards, and apps you want to keep have to be connected again. No AI app can sign you out everywhere or rotate your keys for you; those actions need one of the account's own keys and have no connector tool.
features.editions_note: On Enterprise, Sign out everywhere ends every company session and, by default, every API key and connected app in one audited step.
features.evidence: features.html sign-out; FEATURES.md §7 L755-758, §6 L619-623 (sign-out revokes the parent key and all site sessions); PARITY rows 'Sign out and sign out everywhere', 'Connected apps: list and disconnect', 'Account/credential actions and MCP'.

features.name: Change your sign-in email
features.line: Move the account to another address with a code to the new address and one to the current one; both are needed.
features.who: Anyone leaving a job address or a mailbox they no longer use.
features.how: Under Sign-in, enter the new address. A six-digit code goes to the new address and another to the current one, and both are needed. The account moves to the new address; your handle, sites, and connected apps stay. Every other key on the account is signed out (the one you used stays), and so is every sign-in on your sites. Linked Google sign-ins stay linked and are listed with Unlink.
features.example: A contractor whose agency mailbox is closing moves their account to a personal address before the old one stops receiving mail.
features.where: Sign-in on your sites page, or ask your AI app.
features.limits: Codes are valid for 15 minutes, with three tries, and one change can be pending at a time. The old address gets a notice with a 7-day undo link: undoing puts the account back, signs everything out, and removes sign-ins and connected apps added since the change. An address another account signs in with is refused only after both codes are verified, so asking reveals no more than signing in does. Event and reviewer accounts keep their address. The change needs one of the account's own keys; a connected app cannot make it.
features.editions_note: Enterprise refreshes the stored email from the company's identity provider at each sign-in; a small box with email sign-in turned off has no email to change.
features.evidence: features.html signin-email-change; FEATURES.md §7 L814-836; §6 L672 (EMAIL_SIGNIN=off turns off email change); PARITY row 'Change sign-in email'. Hack: same binary (event accounts refused), not stated separately.

features.name: An email after each sign-in
features.line: After each sign-in or app connection you get one short email saying when, from which browser or app, with a Sign out everywhere link.
features.who: Everyone; it is how you notice a sign-in that was not you.
features.how: After each successful owner sign-in (code, link, or Google) and each app connected on the consent screen, one short email arrives: the time in UTC, the browser or app in a few words ("Chrome on macOS"), and a link to your sites page where Sign out everywhere and the alerts switch are. An app's self-declared name is quoted as "reported by the app" and cut to 40 characters.
features.example: A small business owner sees "Chrome on Windows" in an alert when they only use a Mac, and signs out everywhere before anything is changed.
features.where: Your inbox. Turn it off or on under Sign-in on your sites page.
features.limits: At most one per browser or app a day, and never for API key calls, event accounts, or the plugin reviewer account. It never contains your IP address or a location. Sending happens in the background, so a sign-in never waits on it.
features.editions_note: On Enterprise sign-ins go through the company's identity provider and its audit stream; a small box needs outgoing email set up.
features.evidence: features.html signin-alerts; FEATURES.md §7 L838-849; PARITY row 'Sign-in alert email'. Current page said 'never contains your address or IP'; FEATURES.md says never the IP or a location, so the text now says IP address or location. Hack: same binary, not stated separately.

features.name: Download your data, or delete your account
features.line: One .zip of everything held about you, and a Delete my account that removes the account and all of it at once.
features.who: Anyone leaving, or checking what is kept about them.

areas.title: Notifications
areas.line: A signed call to your receiver or your AI app the moment a visitor writes, and the emails Simple Host sends you.

features.name: A webhook when a visitor writes
features.line: A receiver URL gets a signed POST for record.added, record.changed, file.uploaded, and (Simple Host only) the site events, for one site.
features.who: Anyone who wants Zapier, n8n, Hermes, OpenClaw, or their own receiver to act on new entries or uploads instead of someone checking the page.
features.how: Under Notifications, add an HTTPS receiver address for one site, with an optional label, an optional filter to one storage resource, and an optional custom header for your receiver. Simple Host then POSTs a signed body when a visitor adds a record or KV key (record.added), edits or deletes one (record.changed), or uploads a file (file.uploaded). The body carries the event id, time, site, storage, kind, preset, and the visitor's id or null, plus the table and row or the KV key with its fields, or the file's path, size, and type; visitor-written fields are marked as untrusted. Signatures follow Standard Webhooks (HMAC-SHA256 over the body, timestamp, and id), with matching svix headers. The signing secret is shown once at creation.
features.example: A tutoring business points a webhook at n8n so each new booking row posts a message to their team chat with the lesson time.
features.where: Settings, Notifications on your sites page, or on the team and organiser website screens in Simple Hack, and the REST routes documented at /docs/guides/notifications/.
features.limits: Up to 10 subscriptions per site, about 60 events a minute and 5,000 a day per site, 7 days of delivery history. Five retries over about 10 minutes; sustained failure suspends delivery and emails you once. Public HTTPS addresses only, no redirects, a 5-second timeout. The visitor's email is never in the payload; strings over 2 KB are cut and bodies over 16 KB drop fields and say which. Owner writes never trigger one, and neither do writes to legacy saved data. Offline or taken-down sites skip deliveries.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack offers it on team and organiser websites; Enterprise has its own engine with the same signatures and controls; Simple Hack and Enterprise have the three record events, and site events are Simple Host only; a small box needs its sealing key set, which the installer does by default.

features.name: Site events for your receiver or agent
features.line: A signed call when a version goes live, a domain check changes, someone asks for access, or a visitor signs in for the first time.
features.who: Site owners who want to know that a publish landed, a domain broke or recovered, a client wants into a private site, or a new visitor arrived, without watching the dashboard.
features.how: Under Notifications, tick the site events next to the record events, or name them in the events list over REST or in MCP events/subscribe. site.deployed fires when a version goes live through a deploy or an active-version change (rollback, roll-forward, publishing a saved preview), with version, previous_version, and via. domain.status_changed fires when a domain check records a status different from the previous one (pending, active, error) or a long-failing domain is released, with domain, status, previous_status, reason, and cert. viewer.access_requested fires when a person signed in with an email that is not on a named-viewers list reaches the no-access page, once per person per site per day. visitor.signed_up fires on a person's first sign-in on the site. The last two carry the visitor's id only. The same signatures, retries, and delivery history apply.
features.example: A bookkeeping firm runs a named-viewers client portal and points viewer.access_requested at their team chat; when a client signs in from a work address that is not on the list, they add it before the client has to call.
features.where: Settings, Notifications on your sites page, the events list of POST /v1/sites/{sitename}/notifications, or events/list and events/subscribe over MCP.
features.limits: Simple Host only for now; Simple Hack keeps the three record events and Enterprise has not ported them. An event about the site's owner is never sent. Payloads never carry a visitor's email, IP address, or user agent, or visitor-written text, and have no storage, kind, preset, or untrusted keys; the domain event's reason, cut to 1,024 bytes, may name the addresses the domain points at. A subscription's storage filter narrows record and file events only. The same per-site caps and 7-day history apply. A brand-new site's first version has no subscription yet, so there is no event for it, and a save with publish=false emits nothing.

features.name: A push notification on your phone or computer
features.line: Apple and Google push to a subscribed device, as a third kind of the same notification: you choose which events push and to whom.
features.who: A site owner who wants a push on their phone the moment someone writes, and a signed-in visitor who wants a push when the owner replies to their own entry.
features.how: A push subscription is a row in the same notification engine as webhooks and MCP Events, with the device's endpoint and keys in place of a receiver URL. Both the owner and a signed-in visitor may subscribe their own device site-wide or to one optional resource; a visitor's device is always scoped to record/file events only, never a site-wide or site-level one, and the privacy boundary that keeps it from ever reaching another visitor's data is enforced in delivery itself, not by a required resource. Per-resource controls choose who it reaches (the owner, the row's owner, both, or none) and, optionally, one named column shown as the push text; the default text names no row content. A visitor's device is only ever reached by an event about their own row, key or file, and nothing ever pushes back to whoever made the write, so your own save never pushes to you.

Push endpoints are personal data: never sent to AgentCat or exports, and removed on sign-out, viewer removal, account or site deletion, or erasure.

features.line: Sign-in codes and alerts, email-change notices, a failing domain, idle-site warnings, Submissions digests, and one suspension notice.
features.who: Every account owner; this is the full list of what arrives in your inbox from Simple Host.
features.how: Simple Host emails you for a fixed set of reasons: the six-digit code when you sign in; the code to a new sign-in address and the notice to the old one when you change it; one short alert after each sign-in or app connection (switchable); a confirmation when you delete your account; a notice when a custom domain has been failing for a day; a warning before an idle site is removed and a notice when it is; a digest of new Submissions when you have asked for one (daily, or soon after each arrives, at most one email per name every 10 minutes); and one email if a notification receiver is suspended after sustained failure.
features.example: A bakery owner gets a daily digest of the day's order-form entries and a one-off notice when their domain's DNS record was removed by mistake.
features.where: Your inbox. Sign-in alerts are switched under Sign-in on your sites page; Submissions digests under Email me on the list; idle-site notices can be answered by reply.
features.limits: One-time links in these emails carry their token after a `#`, so it never reaches a server log. Sign-in alerts arrive at most once per browser or app a day and never for API key calls. Idle-site notices reply to support@simple-host.app. There are no marketing emails on this list.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack sends the sign-in and account emails; idle-site warnings and Submissions digests belong to Simple Host sites. Enterprise sends no sign-in emails, since the company's identity provider signs people in. A small box needs outgoing email set up.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §19 L2376-2385 (outbound email list), §19 Delivery row (one owner email on suspension), §7 L838-849 (alerts). Hack and Enterprise email sets not stated in the ranges read; best reading recorded in editions_note. 'No marketing emails' is a reading of the fixed list, stated as 'on this list'.

features.name: A stale-skill notice to agents
features.line: An agent publishing with an older copy of the skill gets a short notice in the reply saying a newer one exists.
features.who: People whose AI agent uses the website-deploy skill, so it keeps up with changes without them noticing.
features.how: The skill tells the API which version it is. When that version is older than the current one, API answers that are JSON objects carry a `_notice` field and an `X-Skill-Notice` header saying so. A plain API call that names no skill version gets nothing.
features.example: A developer's agent publishes a client site with a skill from two months ago; the notice in the reply prompts it to fetch the current one before the next change.
features.where: In the API reply your agent reads; there is nothing to set up.
features.limits: This is the only in-band notice Simple Host sends. Answers that are arrays stay bare, so lists never gain an extra element.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §19 L2385-2387 (stale-skill _notice, X-Skill-Notice, arrays stay bare, only for callers with an older X-Skill-Version). Not stated for Enterprise (separate code base); read as no. Hack: same binary, not stated separately.

features.name: Notification secrets sealed at rest
features.line: Webhook signing secrets and custom header values are encrypted in the database, and the dashboard never shows them again.
features.who: Anyone who cares what a copy of the database would reveal about their receivers.
features.how: Each subscription's signing secret, its previous secret during a rotation, and any custom header value are sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key the operator holds, bound to the row they belong to. Lists never return them; create and rotate show the signing secret once. On a server without the key, new subscriptions are refused, while existing ones can still be removed.
features.example: A SaaS team puts an Authorization header on their webhook so their receiver can trust the call; the header value is stored sealed and never shown in the list.
features.where: Nothing to do on the screen; it applies to every subscription.
features.limits: Without the key, new subscriptions are refused; existing plaintext subscriptions keep delivering until a configured key lets the start-up sweep seal them. The sweep runs for at most 10 seconds at each start and skips rows it could not lock. Rotating a secret the server cannot read ends the previous secret's grace period.
features.editions_note: Enterprise seals with its own separately named key; the standalone Simple Hack package and the small-box installer set the key by default.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §19 L2345 (sealing, refusal without key, start-up sweep 10 seconds, keyless removal, rotation grace), §19 REST delivery row (secrets shown once, never listed); PARITY row 'Notification secret encryption' (Enterprise NOTIFY_ENC_KEY; installers forward the key by default 2026-10-24).

areas.title: Agents and MCP
areas.line: How an AI app or coding agent connects to Simple Host, what it may call, and what it is told while it works.

features.name: Simple Host in your chat app
features.line: Add Simple Host to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code or any AI app once with the one MCP address, then sign in and it can manage your sites.
features.who: Anyone who builds in a chat app rather than a terminal.

ChatGPT: turn on Developer mode under Apps & Connectors, Create, paste the address as the MCP server URL, choose OAuth. Claude Code: `claude mcp add --transport http simple-host <address>`, then `/mcp`, Authenticate. Every other AI app pastes the same address. Each connected app is listed with the device it was connected from and when it was last used. A connected app's sign-in expires after 90 days without use.

features.name: The deploy skill

features.how: The skill is a set of plain instructions your agent reads before it calls Simple Host. It covers sign-up, checking the files, publishing, setting up saved data and visitor sign-in, and opening the live page to confirm it works before saying it is done. It is served with this server's own addresses and limits written in, so an agent on another Simple Host server never reads simple-host.app's numbers.

features.line: Tick which tools you use and which operating system you are on, and it writes out the exact commands to run, with your key ready to copy.

features.name: The connector's tool set
features.line: Most apps see a short core of tools plus a finder that reaches the rest; ChatGPT, OpenAI, and Codex see every operation listed.
features.who: Anyone whose chat app or agent works through the connector.
features.how: The connector has 58 website tools. Apps other than ChatGPT, OpenAI, and Codex are shown a core of 21 (19 building tools plus `find_tools` and `run_tool`); the agent asks `find_tools` for a job and calls what it returns through `run_tool`, and every tool still answers when called by name. ChatGPT, OpenAI, and Codex list every operation individually. `read_site_file` reads up to 10 files in one call and `update_site` can make a small find-and-replace edit without resending the whole file. The server's standing instructions stay under 2,000 characters in every edition.
features.example: A clinic's agent asks for "who visited last week", finds `site_analytics` in one step, and runs it without the person naming the tool.
features.where: Ask your AI app; the full list is on the API page.
features.limits: A call with an argument the tool does not take gets the current schema back and asks you to refresh Simple Host in your app (ChatGPT keeps a connector's tool list from the day it was added). The 19 older saved-data tools removed on 10 October 2026 answer "no longer offered"; their pages keep working. There is no tool for changing your email, rotating your key, signing out everywhere, or deleting your account, by design; `who_am_i` is the only account tool and it reads only.

The task brief said 'a core of 20'; FEATURES.md and PARITY 'MCP tools' say 21 since 2026-10-30, so 21 is used. PARITY row 'MCP instructions length by mode'.

features.name: Visitor tools for a shared site
features.line: Your AI app can read a site someone shared with you and add or change your own entries there, with only the rights a visitor has.
features.who: Anyone a site owner has shared a site with: a client reading a portal, a member filling a form, a judge reading a brief.
features.how: Three tools: `visitor_read_site` lists the sites shared with your email when no address is given, or reads one site's permitted data and page text; `visitor_add_entry` adds an entry; `visitor_change_entry` edits or deletes only your own entry where the site allows it. Each call gets a one-site visitor pass that ends when the call returns, and the site's viewers, passcode, and offline status are checked afresh each time. Other people's names, emails, and account IDs are left out; your own entries are marked `mine`. A site with a passcode takes it as an optional argument under the same lockout rules as the browser.
features.example: A client asks Claude "what did the architect post in my portal this week" and gets the new entries without opening a browser.
features.where: Ask your AI app; the consent screen names visitor access when you connect.
features.limits: You never gain owner powers this way, even on your own site. 200 write attempts per person and site per day across apps. Page text is cut at 256 KiB. Changes made through an app leave a marker naming the app in the site's data history. A passcoded page still needs the passcode to read page text.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack keeps browser sign-in for visitors and offers no visitor tools; Enterprise has none yet.

Small box not stated; same binary.

features.name: Personal details stay out of tool results
features.line: Connector results leave out emails, names, and account IDs unless the owner asks for one submitter by name.
features.who: Everyone whose details pass through a site: visitors, viewers, and the owner.
features.how: `who_am_i` returns your email only when the agent asks for it. Visitors in saved data appear as opaque references scoped to one site, so a count of bookings or a read of entries never resolves anyone's email. Only an owner's request to identify one submitter calls `storage_visitor_emails`, with the references for that entry alone. Viewer changes return only what changed, and signed download and preview links carry no readable internal IDs. The same rules cover Simple Hack results.
features.example: A tutor asks "how many sign-ups this week" and gets a number; later they ask "who booked Tuesday 4 pm" and the agent looks up that one person.
features.where: Built into every connector call; nothing to switch on.
features.limits: Site names, saved-data key names, and your own conversation text are ordinary data and are not hidden from your app.
features.editions_note: Enterprise names colleagues by username because the caller manages that access.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §8 'Data minimisation (2026-10-28)' lead and 'Host MCP privacy (2026-10-28)' paragraph; PARITY L32 (Enterprise: no port, usernames by design). Small box not stated; same binary.

features.name: Agents can find Simple Host on their own
features.line: The homepage reads as markdown, standard discovery files describe the connector and API, and the hosted server is in the MCP registry.
features.who: Agents and crawlers arriving without a person's instructions, and people writing their own integrations.
features.how: Ask the homepage for `text/markdown`, or open `/index.md` or `/llms.md`, and you get the same content as the page in plain text; `/llms.txt` is a short linked quickstart with recipes. The hosted server is listed on registry.modelcontextprotocol.io as `app.simple-host/mcp`, verified by DNS, and also answers at `https://mcp.simple-host.app/mcp` with public DNS records that point agents to it.

features.name: Connector usage analytics
features.line: The hosted service records which connector tools are called and how they went, with secrets, files, and visitor emails removed first.
features.who: The service's own operator, to see which tools agents reach for and where calls fail; it is not a feature anyone switches on for a site.
features.how: On simple-host.app each completed tool call sends one event to AgentCat: the tool name, how long it took, whether it failed and the short error code, the app's name (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, or `other`), a keyed hash in place of the account, the tool's arguments and result (each cut at 8 KB), and the agent's stated intent (cut at 2,048 characters) when the app supplies one. Before sending, passcodes, keys, tokens, signed links, and file contents are replaced, and visitor emails become references. AgentCat removes personal identifiers again before storing. The privacy policy discloses it.
features.example: The operator sees which tools agents reach for most and where calls fail, and tunes the tool set and its hints from that.
features.where: On for simple-host.app only; disclosed on the Privacy page.
features.limits: Off unless a project id is configured. Request headers, screen metadata, and the address you connect from are never sent. Site names, saved-data key names, and conversation text are sent. The passcode screen sends neither arguments nor results.
features.editions_note: Simple Hack, Enterprise, and self-hosted servers are not enrolled and send nothing.

features.name: A refused call says what to do next
features.line: When a tool call is refused, the agent gets the reason, a short code, and one recovery hint chosen for that code.
features.who: Anyone whose agent hits a taken name, a missing sign-in, a quota, or a suspended site mid-task.
features.how: Every refusal carries the server's message, its code (for example `site_exists`, `domain_taken`, `site_quota_reached`, `sign_in_required`, `key_expired`), and one hint matched to that code; the HTTP status picks the hint only when there is no known code. The API returns the same codes, so a skill and a connector see the same thing. An unknown API path or wrong method gets a JSON answer with a link to this server's own reference. A signed-out connection gets the reconnect steps in the error itself.
features.example: An agent tries to create `studio` and is told the name is taken, with the hint to pick another or reuse the existing site, instead of guessing.
features.where: Your agent sees it; a good agent tells you in plain words.
features.limits: Pages people visit still get HTML error pages, never JSON.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §8 Errors and API transport errors rows, MCP tools row (reconnect steps ride on the signed-out error); PARITY rows 'MCP error hints', 'API route errors'.

features.name: The agent asks before anything irreversible
features.line: Every skill and the connector tell the agent to ask you before a site goes online, before deleting, and before widening who sees data.
features.who: Anyone letting an agent work on their sites without watching every step.
features.how: Before a new site goes online for the first time the agent asks once, naming the site, its address, and that anyone with the link can open it. It always asks before deleting a site or data, making private data public, changing who can see or save, connecting a domain, rolling back, or taking a site offline. Updates you asked for in the same conversation go ahead without a second question. The skills, `llms.txt`, and the connector's own instructions all say the same.
features.example: An agent updating a restaurant's prices does it straight away, but asks before switching the reservations list from private to public.
features.where: Built into the skills and the connector instructions.
features.limits: Whether the question reaches you depends on your app following its instructions; the server itself does not block the call.
features.evidence: FEATURES.md §9 L986-992 (INTENT 2026-09-28 ask-first rules in skills, llms.txt and server instructions). Enterprise not stated; same rule carried in its own skills by best reading.

features.name: Out-of-date agents are told to update
features.line: If your agent works from an old copy of the skill, the service tells it so as it works, rather than letting it fail later.
features.who: Anyone who installed the skills months ago and forgot.
features.how: A skill names its version on each call. When that version is older than the current one, the answer carries a short notice asking the agent to refresh its skills, and a matching response header. A plain API call that names no skill gets nothing. It is the only notice the service puts into a response this way.
features.example: A marketing agency's agent installed in spring publishes fine in autumn but is told to update, and the one-line install brings the current recipes.
features.where: Your agent sees it and should mention it to you.
features.limits: Whether you hear about it is up to your agent: nothing is shown on any screen.
features.editions_note: Enterprise refuses an obsolete skill outright instead of warning.

areas.title: Admin and operations
areas.line: What the operator can see and do, the rules every account and visitor meets, and how to run a copy of the software yourself.

features.name: The operator console
features.line: One signed-in page where the operator sees accounts, sites, and API traffic, and acts on any site or account.
features.who: Whoever runs the service: the operator of simple-host.app, an event organiser on their own box, or company IT.
features.how: The console has six tabs. Overview: accounts, new in 7 and 30 days, live sites, storage and disk used, the latest sign-ups with their source, the 10 biggest websites, and network use for the month (bytes in and out against the allowance, bytes served per website, split pages and API). Users: a searchable table with each person's sites and sign-up source, New key (replaces a participant's keys with one new key, shown once), Suspend or Re-enable, and Delete (the same erasure a person gets from Delete my account). Sites: every site in one sortable table (recently created, recently updated, size, most views by people in 30 days), 50 rows a page, with a menu per row for Open, Analytics, Versions, Data (lists, rows, CSV), Connect or Disconnect domain, Take down or Restore, and Delete. API: calls per day by kind, new accounts and sites per day with the change against the previous period, a world map shaded by API calls per country with the top 10 beside it, then today's calls, callers, errors, routes. Moderation: taken-down sites with Restore, an idle-site dry run (would warn, would remove), and a saved-data watch. Tools: issue participant accounts in bulk and download entries. The operator can read any site's analytics and download every site with its data as one archive. Every search box takes several words, all must match, and a `-word` hides rows that match it.
features.example: An event organiser running their own box issues forty participant accounts before a hackathon, then watches the API tab fill as teams start publishing.
features.where: The operator's console, signed in with the admin key or as the admin user. It is not linked from public pages.
features.limits: Only requests that match a real API route are counted; the server's own health checks are kept apart as 'from this server'. API calls are counted per country with no address stored; growth data is pruned at 400 days. The admin never reads a site's passcode; it can remove one for moderation. Wrong admin keys count against a rate limit, so 'Too many tries' is real.
features.editions_note: Enterprise's admin page is for company IT: disable or enable a person, offboard by email, access requests, export, revoke a leaked key, and a 'This instance' panel (release, pending migrations, bucket check, limits in force). On the hosted hackathon instance the console also has an Events table.

The owner's product knowledge server (§11 'Owner product knowledge') left out on instruction. Not linked: /admin is owner-only.

features.name: Take-down and suspension
features.line: The operator can take a site down or suspend an account, reversibly, with the reason shown and nothing deleted.
features.who: Visitors and owners of a site the operator has acted on, and operators handling an abuse report.
features.how: A taken-down site answers 'This site has been taken down' on every address it had (its site host, its person path, its claimed name, and its custom domain). The owner sees the reason on their dashboard. The owner's key can still read and export the site; deploys, renames, visibility changes, and data writes are refused. A suspended person's key, connected apps, and visitor sessions stop working with the reason, sign-in is refused, and their sites go down. Nothing is deleted. Restore or re-enable reverses it; a site taken down on its own stays down when its owner is re-enabled.
features.example: A page impersonating a bank is reported on a Sunday; the operator takes it down within the hour, the owner sees the reason, and nothing is lost if the appeal succeeds.
features.where: The take-down page a visitor sees; the reason on the owner's dashboard and site cards.
features.limits: A suspended site keeps everything and is kept past the Recently deleted window. The take-down page loads nothing and carries no link. Appeals are read by a person within 30 days (see Terms, privacy, and support).
features.editions_note: Enterprise restricts a site to its owner with a reason instead; the owner cannot raise, rename, or move it, and only an admin's Lift restores it.

It carries an emergency-services line and, for child sexual abuse material, says not to include the material. The report is emailed to the support contact with the reporter as the reply-to address. It is linked from the footer of every page (so the 404 page too), the home page, the terms, and the support page.

Five reports per address, then one every 10 minutes, and 60 an hour in all. Nothing is stored; the server log keeps only the reason and the host. The offline and take-down pages carry no link to it.

Intimate images are removed within 48 hours of a valid request. Appeals are open for 30 days and a person reads each one and gives one answer. Adverse changes get 14 days' notice. The DMCA agent is registered (DMCA-1081064) with support@simple-host.app as the directory contact. The privacy page describes member emails, role-based judging access, private team results, and archive retention on Simple Hack, and the support page explains reconnecting an AI app for the right role and revoking connections with Sign out everywhere.

features.name: Sign-ups by source
features.line: Each account records once, when it is made, where it came from: the website, which AI app, or an agent, never an address.
features.who: The operator reading where new accounts come from; every account holder, as a matter of what is recorded about them.

The method is recorded too (emailed code, Google, issued by an operator). A campaign tag or link carried in the same visit (`?from=` and `utm_*` values, the referring host, the landing time) is kept as detail; there is no attribution cookie and no cross-visit window. The operator's Overview groups sign-ups by source over the last week, the last 30 days, and all time, and each group opens to its accounts with a funnel (signed up, connected an AI, published a site, got visitors), search, and a CSV download.

features.name: Rate limits that tell you when to retry
features.line: Every limited request answers with RateLimit headers and an exact Retry-After, so a script knows the balance and the wait.
features.who: Anyone writing a script or agent against the API, and the operator setting limits on their own copy.
features.how: Limits are token buckets per address or per account. Responses carry `RateLimit`, `RateLimit-Policy`, `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset`: the remaining balance after the request and the seconds until one more token is available. A refused request answers 429 with the code `rate_limited` and a real `Retry-After`. Unknown API paths and unsupported methods answer JSON with a code and a docs hint; website pages keep their HTML 404.
features.example: A booking site's nightly export script reads RateLimit-Remaining and paces itself instead of guessing.
features.where: On every limited API response; the values in force are stated in the API reference.
features.limits: Saved-data reads are limited per site and address, or per account for a signed-in key or connector. Items added to a list without the owner's key: 30 a minute per address. Uploads, sign-in, emails, and the connector have their own buckets. Every user-facing limit is a setting on your own copy.
features.editions_note: Enterprise runs per-pod buckets plus shared counters across pods for sign-in, hand-off, key mint, and the connector, and reports the same headers.

features.name: Size caps, blocked files, and reserved names
features.line: Plain limits on what a site, a file, or an account can hold, with a stable error code when one is hit.
features.who: Anyone publishing a large site or storing data, and anyone picking a name.
features.how: A site archive is capped at 100 MB; a few accounts have a higher cap by arrangement. A site's live saved data may grow to 50 MB; past that, only growth is refused, with the code `site_full`. Shared state is 1 MB, a list item 64 KB, and one update may carry at most 100 operations. An account may hold **100 sites**. Uploads of blocked file types are refused. Handles and subdomain names that would collide with the service's own addresses are reserved, `report` among them. Every page carries the standard security headers, and the service's own pages run under a strict content security policy.
features.example: A photographer's portfolio comes in at 160 MB; the error names the 100 MB cap, so they resize the images or use the photo flow, which stores small copies.
features.where: The error message names the cap in force; the API reference lists them.
features.limits: Caps are stated where they apply, and the served text follows the value in force on that server. The owner of a copy can raise or lower each one.
features.editions_note: Enterprise caps sites and stored bytes per owner and shows usage on the dashboard.

features.name: Safe retries with an Idempotency-Key
features.line: A create call sent twice with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the first answer for 24 hours, so a retried script makes one site.
features.who: Anyone deploying from CI or an agent that may retry on a dropped connection.
features.how: Owner create calls (site archives and inline files, photos, domain bindings, named viewers, export links, version preview links, notification subscriptions, storage download links, and table row creates) accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header. The same account, route, key, and body replay the original status and body, including errors, for 24 hours; concurrent duplicates wait for the first answer. List adds and state updates take the header too for signed-in callers.
features.example: A deploy pipeline times out on the first publish and retries; the second call returns the same version instead of a duplicate.
features.where: An optional header on create calls, in the API reference.
features.limits: A different body under the same key answers 409 `idempotency_key_reused`. Replays are kept in memory on simple-host.app and are lost on a restart. Rate limits and sign-in still apply to a replay, and replaying a link does not renew its expiry. Anonymous writes ignore the header.
features.editions_note: Enterprise keeps replays in its database across pods and answers 422 on a changed body.

features.name: Judging
features.line: A weighted rubric, judges spread openly, automatically, by hand, or by track panel, conflicts of interest, a lock, and published results.
features.who: Judges scoring from a phone, and organisers running the rubric, assignments, and results.
features.how: The organiser sets a rubric of 1 to 10 criteria, each with a weight and a points scale, before judging opens; a new event starts with Idea, Execution, Design, and Demo at 25 percent each, scored 1 to 5. Judges are spread openly (everyone scores everyone), automatically (an even, conflict-aware spread), by manual assignment, or by panels per track. A judge or an organiser can declare a conflict of interest, which drops that pairing from queues and totals. Organisers, including co-organisers, can also judge under their own account, with the same conflicts and locks. The judge's queue puts the least-covered team first, the scoring screen opens the frozen team site and saves criteria as you go, and Save and next moves on. The organiser watches coverage on the dashboard, locks judging, then publishes: ties are flagged and can be resolved by hand, totals can be raw or normalised across judges, and public ranks and scores can each be hidden. After publication each team privately sees its total, rank, and the judges' comments without names.
features.example: A corporate innovation day with 30 teams and 9 judges uses automatic assignment, a sponsor's engineer declares a conflict with the team he mentored, and the organiser publishes winners only.
features.where: Manage, Judging for organisers; the judge link and Judge entries for judges; or ask your AI app with the judge role.
features.limits: Scoring opens only once entries close. Rubric weights must sum to 100; the rubric cannot change while judging is locked, and removing scored criteria or lowering points below saved scores asks for confirmation. Unlocking requires a reason, which is logged. Automatic assignment includes organisers only when Include organisers is ticked. Public results never show individual judge scores or comments. Results CSV and scores CSV can be downloaded at any time.
